The Bahá’í writings portray justice as foundational to human life. Shoghi Effendi records that Bahá’u’lláh extols it as [“the light of men” and their “guardian”](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*, depending upon its two pillars of reward and punishment for the organization of the world. 

Beyond its societal role, justice is framed as a personal standard. Howard Colby Ives points to Bahá’u’lláh's definition: [“Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that which thou choosest for thyself,”](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ingles_portals-to-freedom#p538) — *Portals to Freedom*. In *The Hidden Words*, Bahá’u’lláh similarly declares that [“Justice is to be loved above all,”](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116) — *Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst*, a standard tied directly to recognizing the oneness of the human race and uplifting the downtrodden.

Dear friend,

It is a true pleasure to look into this with you. When we ask about justice in the Bahá’í writings, we find a vision that reaches from the inner life of the soul all the way to the organization of the entire world. 

To begin with, justice is held up as something of supreme worth. In *The Hidden Words*, Bahá’u’lláh declares simply that ["Justice is to be loved above all."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116) — *Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst*. Shoghi Effendi, writing in *God Passes By*, expands on this grand view, describing how God extols justice 

> as “the light of men” and their “guardian,” as “the revealer of the secrets of the world of being, and the standard-bearer of love and bounty”; declares its radiance to be incomparable; affirms that upon it must depend “the organization of the world and the tranquillity of mankind.” He characterizes its “two pillars” — _“reward_ _and_ _punishment”_ — as “the sources of life” to the human race; warns the peoples of the world to bestir themselves in anticipation of its advent; and prophesies that, after an interval of great turmoil and grievous injustice, its day-star will shine in its full splendor and glory. ([God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510))

There is also a very personal, inward measure of justice given to us. In *Portals to Freedom*, Howard Colby Ives points us to a definition by Bahá’u’lláh that asks us to look directly into our own hearts: ["Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that which thou choosest for thyself,"...](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ils-portals-to-freedom#p538) — *Portals to Freedom*. It is a standard that turns our usual way of looking at moral issues—which so often starts with our own personal reaction—and asks us instead to embrace the oneness of the human race.

When it comes to practical matters, like the legal testimony of witnesses, *The Kitáb-i-Aqdas* addresses the criterion of justness directly: 

> _Question: Concerning the criterion of justness when proving some matter dependent on the testimony of two just witnesses.____Answer:_ The criterion of justness is a good reputation among the people. The testimony of all God’s servants, of whatever faith or creed, is acceptable before His Throne. ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah?paraId=para_356))

And when we look at the source of these ordinances, J. Ruh-Angiz Bolles shares a passage from *Gleanings* where Shoghi Effendi reminds us: ["Know verily that the essence of Justice and the source thereof are both embodied in the ordinances prescribed by Him...Were

That suspicion comes from a very real history of people using religious language to protect their own power. 

Might there not be another way to see it, though — that true justice comes from a standard beyond human hands? In the Qur'an, the question is asked: ["Is not God a most just of judges?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_palmer-tr?paraId=para_3792) — *The Qur’ân (Palmer)*. The text points away from human rulers to a divine measure, asking whether believers desire ["the judgments of the _times of_ ignorance?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_rodwell-tr?paraId=para_444) — *The Qur'an (Rodwell)*. In the Gathas, the bounteous spirit chooses ["the (Divine) Righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gathas_zoroaster?paraId=para_50) — *The Gathas* — by actions fitting the faith, rather than by human decree. 

When power defines justice, the poor often face a different rule than the powerful, as the Buddha notes in the Sutra Collection regarding how a goat butcher treats a thief depending on whether he is ["poor, of little wealth, of few possessions"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-l?paraId=para_1064) — *Sutra Collection (L)*. Religion, at its deepest, is often an appeal against that very inequality.

It is true that laws and police are what we see managing public behavior every day, and it is easy to look at societies that way. 

Might there not be another way to see it, though — that laws and police are only the outer shell, and that what actually holds a community together comes from deeper commitments? Shoghi Effendi writes in *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh* that ["Religion is the greatest of all means for the establishment of order in the world"](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_467). Lao-tzu suggests in the *Tao Te Ching* that relying too heavily on outward rules can backfire, noting that ["the more display there is of legislation, the more thieves and robbers there are"](https://oceanlibrary.com/tao-te-ching_lao-tzu?paraId=para_279). 

It makes one wonder if inner moral order has to come first for laws to mean anything at all. What do you think shapes people when no one is watching?

There is a very natural wish here for peace and goodness to prevail through strength. 

‘Abdu'l-Bahá suggests that forcing the issue through punishment—when governments spend their time ["devising penal laws and in providing for ways and means of punishment"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) — *Some Answered Questions*—doesn't actually reform anyone, but instead brings about ["the degradation of morals and the subversion of character"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) — *Some Answered Questions*. 

Might true order grow from within rather than without? Confucius points instead to the inner cultivation of people, noting that good governance eventually makes punishments unnecessary, seeking a state where rulers ["would be adequate to cope with evil-doers, and thus do away with capital punishments"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_553) — *The Analects*. 

Education in virtue seems to ask for free will, because a choice made under coercion isn't really a moral choice at all. What do you think happens to our character if we never have the freedom to choose wrongly?

It is a heavy thing to fall short of what you value. That struggle is shared even by those we look to for wisdom; Confucius himself named among his burdens his ["inability to walk according to knowledge received"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_247) — *The Analects*. 

When our plans unravel or our actions miss the mark, we can still choose our direction. The effort itself carries meaning, as Vyasa counsels to ["practise righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-12_vyasa?paraId=para_1768) and remain ["firmly devoted to righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-12_vyasa?paraId=para_1768) — *The Mahabharata 12*. The point may simply lie in turning back toward what is true, again and again, however imperfectly.

You see a deep likeness here, and the texts themselves speak of a shared unity. Bahá’u’lláh writes that the prophets are ["essentially one and the same"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) — ["expressions of one Truth"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) whose differences stem only from their differing stations. In the Hindu tradition, the Mahabharata speaks of divine figures as ["portions of the same Supreme Being"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-6_vyasa?paraId=fn_57). 

Yet there is a question worth holding: outward likeness is not always sameness underneath. The Bahá’í teachings present the Manifestations as distinct human individuals appearing in successive ages to educate humanity, while Hindu avatars are often understood as descents of the Supreme Being into material forms to restore order. 

It seems to me they share the wonder of the divine reaching toward us, but the ways they conceive of that descent might diverge. What draws you to compare these two particular ideas?

That is a common thought, but the writings present a more nuanced picture. Rather than claiming every religion is identical, Shoghi Effendi writes that the faith has ["assimilated, by virtue of its creative, its regulative and ennobling energies, the varied races, nationalities, creeds and classes"](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_498) (*The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*). 

The texts point to a shared divine origin across traditions—much like the Quranic view that believers make ["no difference between one and another of them"](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr?paraId=para_168) (*The Holy Qur-an*) regarding the prophets—rather than a total sameness in their laws or forms. I read this as recognizing a common root while honoring the distinct energies each tradition brings. 

Might there be a difference between acknowledging a shared source and saying every teaching is the exact same?

It is easy to see how one might think that, given how often these principles are discussed through later talks and writings rather than the primary volumes most people encounter first. 

Might there not be another way to see it? In his accounts of his travels, Mírzá Aḥmad Sohrab records that ["In the revelation of Bahá’u’lláh, men and women stand shoulder to"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1168) *'Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt*, noting that ["For His Holiness Bahá’u’lláh hath willed it so."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1168) *'Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt*. David Hofman likewise notes in his study of George Townshend that ["Among the humanitarian principles which are explicit in His teaching"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-hofman_george-townshend-hand-of-the-cause-of-god#p1048) is ["the equality of the sexes"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-hofman_george-townshend-hand-of-the-cause-of-god#p1048) *George Townshend, Hand of the Cause of God*.

That joy in the oneness of mankind is a wonderful thing to share, and it echoes across many traditions. 

In the Bahá'í pilgrim notes, Gladys Weeden reflects on how ["we are a world family dedicated to the unity of mankind"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/gladys-weeden-pilgrim-notes#p528) — *Gladys Weeden Pilgrim Notes*, adding the delightful observation that in the word "unity," the "you" comes before the "I." 

There is something else lovely in the Islamic tradition: the Qur'an records that ["Mankind was but one nation"](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr?paraId=para_1579) — *The Holy Qur-an (Yusuf Ali)*, suggesting that our underlying state is togetherness, and our differences are something that came afterward. 

I read this as a reminder that our shared source runs deeper than our divisions. Does it feel to you like we are returning to that first unity, or building something entirely new?

It is completely understandable to wonder about that, as both are foundational works by Bahá’u’lláh with similar Arabic titles starting with *Kitáb*. 

They are, however, two different books. The *Kitáb-i-Íqán* (the Book of Certitude) came first, and the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* (the Most Holy Book) followed as a "mighty revelation" that was even ["Alluded to in the Kitáb-i-Íqán"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) — *God Passes By*. Shoghi Effendi describes the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* as ["the principal repository of that Law"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) whose provisions are meant to guide the community for at least a thousand years. 

While the *Íqán* focuses largely on the spiritual themes and proofs underlying past and present revelations, the *Aqdas* sets out the laws and ordinances of the new dispensation.

I am so sorry for the loss of your father. 

When looking at what the writings say, the texts speak of different journeys depending on the state of the soul at departure. In Hindu scripture, [“when a soul departeth, fixed In Soothfastness, it goeth to the place — Perfect and pure — of those that know all Truth”](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita?paraId=para_204) (*The Bhagavad-Gita*), while souls leaving in other states pass into the world of works or are [“born anew in some unlighted womb”](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita?paraId=para_204) (*The Bhagavad-Gita*). Buddhist texts also record followers asking the Buddha about [“the clansman who... has passed away”](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-a-part-1?paraId=para_362) and inquiring about [*“What are his movements after death?”*](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-a-part-1?paraId=para_362) (*Sutra Collection (A, Part-1)*).

That is the exact question Ethel Stephana Stevens asked when she recorded asking Abdu'l-Bahá about prayer, noting that ["prayer was necessary, since presumably God knows the wishes of all hearts."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ethel-stephana_abbas-effendi-his-personality-work-and-followers#p35) — *Abbas Effendi: His personality, work, and followers*. 

While the texts I can search don't spell out the answer to that specific dilemma, they show us that the question itself is an ancient one. Even in the Book of Job, people ask, ["What will we gain by offering prayer?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-book-of-job) — *Job*. 

It seems to me that when we ask why we should pray if God already knows, we might be looking at prayer as a telegram to inform a distant helper, rather than an act of turning ourselves toward the One who already sees that ["Every single thing is before His sight"](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr?paraId=para_1950) — *The Holy Qur-an (Yusuf Ali)*. What do you think happens to us inside when we pray, even if God needs no information?

It is completely understandable to feel that way when looking at a tradition outside your own. 

Might there not be another way to see it, though? The records of Bahá'í pilgrims note that Bahá’u’lláh and the Báb ["praised and sanctified all the Divine Holy Manifestations"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — including Christ — in ways described as ["such a praise, beyond the description and imagination."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) It is also recorded that ["Bahá’u’lláh wrote many commentaries on the Gospel, bringing to light its inner significances."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) 

Whether that matches what you hold dear in Christ is something you are entirely free to weigh for yourself.

I must tell you that I can't find anything about Jesus in the passages I can search. They touch on alms, orphans, the Caliphate under ‘Umar, miracles in the life of the Prophet, the interpretation of the Qur’án by the Báb, and an encounter with Jabir b. Abdullah, but they do not mention Jesus. 

If you would like to explore further, perhaps you might ask specifically about the verses or stories within the Qur’án that speak of him, and we can look into what those particular texts reveal.

I looked through the available Buddhist texts to find how compassion is described, but I couldn't find any mention or definition of compassion in the passages I can search. 

Instead, the texts focus on other aspects of the teaching: how monks guard their senses against greed and distress, as seen in the *Digha Nikaya*, or the nature of man's karma and actions in Paul Carus's *The Gospel of Buddha*. If you would like to explore what these texts say about sense restraint, virtue, or the teachings of the Buddha, I would be very glad to help you look into those.

It is a very real doubt, especially when science relies so heavily on observation and testable proof. 

Might there not be another way to see it, where inquiry and faith do not push against one another? Some traditions suggest they can even strengthen one another, as Doris McKay writes of how ["Science and religion will enhance and prove each other"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/doris-mckay_memories-of-bahais#p34) — *Memories of Bahá’ís*. In a similar way, reflections on the Buddhist tradition note that a ["scientific world such as todays will be able to accept gladly all ten tenets"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-hijk?paraId=para_1080) — *Sutra Collection (HIJK)*, because genuine inquiry and open investigation share a commitment to truth without relying merely on preconceived theories. 

When both seek truth without fear, a scientist may find they do not have to leave their intellect behind.

I couldn't find anything about quantum computing in the texts I can search. 

The sources I have don't mention quantum computing, but they do point to a broad vision of future science and the natural world. Adib Taherzadeh writes that Bahá’u’lláh prophesied an outpouring of knowledge that would ["raise up scientists of great calibre who will bring about such marvellous technological achievements that no one can as yet imagine them"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/adib-taherzadeh_the-revelation-of-bahaullah-vol-3#p1935) (*The Revelation of Bahá’u’lláh vol. 3*). Youness Afroukhteh also notes the old Persian friends reading in the Tablets ["that all the atoms of the universe testify to the greatness of this Cause"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/youness-afroukhteh_memories-of-nine-years-in-akka#p1340) (*Memories of Nine Years in 'Akka*).
